transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-01-07 11:30 AM PST | Duration: 58m
Attendees: Alex Moran (Redwood AE), Priya Nair (Redwood SE), Jordan Patel (Keystone VP Eng), Maya Rivera (Platform), Sam Liu (Head of ML), Renee Fox (SRE)

Summary: Discovery focused on reserved GPU commitment for predictable throughput, tenant isolation requirements, and a realistic burst strategy for periodic traffic spikes. Customer wants a pilot that proves cost/perf tradeoffs and verifies KMS + VPC integration for compliance.

Topics: reserved capacity sizing, prewarm/warm pool behavior, eviction and failover, VPC and KMS integration, SOC 2/compliance questions, benchmark run planning.

[00:00] Alex: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Alex from Redwood. Quick intros, then Priya will walk through how Dedicated works and we can get into your spike and isolation needs.
[00:18] Jordan: Hi, Jordan here. Thanks. We're trying to understand whether we should go hosted for now or commit to reserved GPUs because our prediction API has real spikes during daily batch jobs.
[00:26] Maya: Hey all, Maya — we run a multi-tenant inference layer, most traffic is embeddings and convo generation for search, we care a lot about tail latency.
[00:34] Priya: Cool, could you share baseline numbers — qps distributions, 95/99 latencies?
[00:38] Sam: Sure, rough numbers: steady state 200 rps, but daily spikes up to 6k rps for about 6-8 minutes when a nightly reindex runs; 95th ~ 120ms, 99th ~ 450ms now but we're trying to get 99th under 350ms.
[00:58] Renee: Also, we have strict isolation — certain customers require tenancy isolation and we have to attest keys never leave our KMS.
[01:05] Alex: Great — that feeds into whether Dedicated with tenant fencing makes sense. Priya, want to jump into topology options?
[01:12] Priya: Yeah. So Redwood Dedicated provides reserved GPU pools that you can pin to your org — think reserved nodes. For spikes we support warm pools/hot nodes and burst into shared capacity as a fallback. We also support a private deployment path if you need the entire control plane in your V P C or on-prem.
[01:32] Jordan: When you say warm pool, how long does a warm VM stay ready? Prewarm latency is our biggest unknown.
[01:39] Priya: By default prewarm cookie is 5–15 minutes depending on model size. For prewarmed GPU contexts we maintain KV cache warmup for pinned models; if you want aggressive prewarm we recommend reserving a small hotpool. There's a tradeoff: cost for always-warm nodes vs slightly higher tail latency and burst fallbacks.
[02:03] Jordan: How does fallback to hosted shared capacity affect latency? We can't afford massive tail increases.
[02:08] Priya: Fallback path routes to compatible quantized variants that have lower memory but slightly higher latency. In practice we've seen tail increase ~15–30% in worst case for the fallback path, but it depends on model architecture.
[02:27] Sam: Is quantization automatically applied? We need to ensure output quality doesn't degrade for ranking models.
[02:33] Priya: It's opt-in. Redwood Optimize can recommend quant profiles per workload; you can pin full-precision variants for critical routes.
[02:40] Maya: On isolation, do you support node-level fencing so tenant A can't evict tenant B?
[02:46] Priya: Yes — dedicated nodes can be single-tenant or soft-isolated with strict cgroups and GPU MIG/sharing rules. For the strictest requirement we'd advise physical isolation: dedicated nodes only for that tenant.
[02:58] Jordan: Ok. For our compliance team, encryption and KMS: we want customer-managed keys and audit logs. Can Redwood join our KMS?
[03:05] Alex: We integrate with customer KMS via our private deployment or via KMS connectors for Dedicated. We can do envelope encryption where your keys sign and unwrap tokens; logs are pushed to your SIEM. We'll send the architecture doc.
[03:20] Renee: Do you support HSM-backed keys?
[03:23] Priya: Yes, we support customer-managed HSM/KMS providers — H S M-backed envelopes are possible with the private path.
[03:30] Jordan: Network constraints — our egress rules are strict, so V P C peering or private networking is required.
[03:35] Alex: For Dedicated we can either place the nodes in a shared managed VPC with strict peering and firewall rules or run Private with customer VPC where the control plane is isolated.
[03:46] Maya: Cost — what's the rough monthly cost for reserving X of the node types? We have a mix of L13 and L40-style GPUs in our self-host currently.
[03:55] Alex: I'll send the SKU/pricing matrix after this call. Prices vary a lot by GPU class and prewarm strategy. We'll include examples with cost per million tokens for typical generation and embedding mixes.
[04:08] Jordan: What's the expected lead time to get a Dedicated pool provisioned? We need predictability for go-live planning.
[04:12] Priya: Provisioning takes about 3–5 business days for standard regions; private/on-prem is longer depending on network approvals. For reserved capacity with standard nodes we can speed to 48–72 hours if quotas are available.
[04:24] Sam: We need an S L A on latency and throughput — can you commit to 99th latency S L O s on reserved pools?
[04:31] Priya: We offer SLA-backed uptime and throughput for Dedicated. Latency SLOs are more workload-dependent; we instrument and provide per-route latency dashboards and can set contractual SLOs tied to reserved capacity.
[04:43] Jordan: For the spike scenario — 6k rps for 6–8 minutes — what's your recommendation for reserve sizing vs warm pool?
[04:51] Priya: Best practice: reserve enough capacity to serve your 95th percentile and use hotpool to absorb the upper tail. For a 6k spike, if steady is 200 rps, that's about 30x — you'd either size for the spike which is expensive, or reserve a baseline and allow burst with prewarmed nodes that scale in seconds. We can run a simulation.
[05:10] Priya: Another pattern is reserving a small hotpool per region and configuring autoscale rules that prewarm additional nodes when queue depth exceeds thresholds.
[05:20] Renee: Does autoscale require control plane callbacks to our infra? We need to avoid public internet callbacks.
[05:25] Alex: We support webhook callbacks over private networking or an agent that can run in your V P C; both are supported in Private or hybrid setups.
[05:33] Jordan: How deterministic is prewarm time for big models (8–12B)? The KV cache load takes longer.
[05:38] Priya: For 8–12B models warmup is typically 20–90 seconds for KV cache to be warm if we stream the prefix; a full model cold start can be 90–300s depending on quantization and topology. Prewarmed contexts reduce that drastically.
[05:55] Sam: For our reranker model we cannot lose exactness from quantization; we want zero delta in ranking performance. Can we route rerank to full-precision dedicated nodes and other less-critical calls to quantized fallback?
[06:05] Priya: Absolutely — routing by policy is supported. You can pin critical routes to specific nodes or model variants.
[06:11] Maya: On monitoring and observability: are token-level costs and latency breakdowns available per route?
[06:16] Alex: Yes, Redwood Console provides per-route token-level cost breakdowns, trace spans and KV cache hits, and a change history for model rollouts. We'll show screenshots in the follow-up doc.
[06:27] Jordan: Procurement questions — contract length and commit discounts?
[06:31] Alex: Dedicated contracts usually have monthly or annual reserved commits. Longer terms get deeper discounts and capacity priority. We'll include a pricing cadence.
[06:40] Maya: A technical deep dive will be needed for our infra team — can Priya or someone do an e2e on our network next week?
[06:46] Priya: Yes, happy to. Maybe an SE-to-SE deep benchmark where we run your models.
[06:51] Jordan: Let's talk about failure modes — if a reserved node fails during a spike, how do you ensure traffic doesn't starve?
[06:57] Priya: We have smart routing and fallback — the system redistributes traffic to other reserved nodes and automatically spins fallback into shared or private nodes depending on policy. There's also a grace period where we hold requests in a queue with partial responses if the model supports streaming.
[07:13] Sam: Do you provide canary and A/B rollouts for model swaps? We want to swap quant profiles gradually.
[07:18] Alex: Yes — Canary and A/B are supported with percentage-based rollouts and automatic rollback if quality or latency regressions are detected.
[07:25] Renee: Auditing — do you keep immutable audit logs for inference requests? Our compliance needs at least 90 days of detailed audit trails.
[07:33] Priya: We can push detailed logs to your logging endpoint or store them encrypted; retention policies are configurable. For Private deployments you keep full control of logs.
[07:44] Jordan: Can we see a runbook for eviction behavior and tenant quarantining?
[07:49] Priya: We'll share our eviction playbook. Short answer: reserve nodes are least likely to be preempted; in edge cases we have preemption policies and quarantining that move noisy tenants to separate tenancy before underlying eviction.
[08:02] Alex: Ok let's get concrete. Sam, can you outline what success looks like for the pilot?
[08:07] Sam: Pilot success: 1) prove we can hit 99th <= 350ms during a simulated daily spike, 2) verify KMS integration and that keys are customer-managed, 3) show cost delta vs hosted + fallbacks, and 4) confirm we can isolate high-risk tenants.
[08:22] Alex: That's clear. Priya, we'll need to provision a test Dedicated pool and run a 24hr spike sim on your harness.
[08:28] Priya: I'll need the model tarballs, traffic pattern, and VPC details. We'll run a workload with your exact mix and capture per-route traces.
[08:36] Jordan: About model tarballs — we have some legal constraints on sharing models. Could we run the benchmark with a synthetic but representative workload?
[08:44] Priya: Yes, synthetic traces are fine; if you can't share model weights, we can run with a trace-driven load using reference models to mimic token distributions.
[08:53] Maya: For the synthetic run, what metrics will you capture?
[08:56] Priya: We'll capture p50/p95/p99 latencies, CPU/GPU utilization, KV cache hit rate, tokens per second, and cost per million tokens. Also tail behavior during prewarm and cold start.
[09:10] Renee: Our legal wants data residency controls — all inference logs for EU customers must stay in eu-west1. Can you pin region?
[09:17] Alex: Yes — region pinning is supported. For strict residency we'd advise Private deployment in the region or a dedicated regional pool.
[09:26] Jordan: There's one more question — can you integrate with our existing SSO (SAML) and RBAC?
[09:31] Priya: Yes, we support SAML/SSO and fine-grained RBAC with audit trails.
[09:36] Sam: Another micro question — tokenization differences across models can affect cost. How do you normalize token accounting?
[09:43] Alex: We normalize to UTF-8 token accounting and provide per-model token multipliers. We'll include tokenization examples in the cost sheet.
[09:52] Jordan: Ok great. Any showstoppers from Redwood?
[09:55] Alex: None so far. We think this is a good fit for a pilot. We'll produce a concrete plan and timeline.
[10:02] Priya: For the spike sim, propose: we reserve baseline capacity for 500 rps, spin a hotpool sized to absorb up to 3k rps, and allow fallback into shared up to 6k while we tune prewarm thresholds. Then iterate after the first run.
[10:19] Jordan: Sounds reasonable. We'll review and provide the model mix.
[10:22] Maya: For compliance review — send SOC 2 and our legal will follow up.
[10:26] Alex: Will do. I'll attach the compliance pack and pricing sheet.
[10:31] Renee: One operational ask — can you provide a maintenance window cadence and notifications for node updates?
[10:36] Priya: Yes, maintenance windows are configurable; reserved customers get scheduled windows and advance notice.
[10:41] Sam: If the pilot succeeds, what's typical lead time to full conversion?
[10:45] Alex: Typically a few weeks to a couple months depending on contract, provisioning, and network approvals.
[10:50] Jordan: Ok let's wrap.
[10:52] Alex: Quick recap of next steps: Alex sends pricing and compliance docs; Priya runs the synthetic spike plan and coordinates benchmarks; Sam shares model mix and SLOs; Renee shares VPC constraints. We'll reconvene after initial benchmark.
[11:06] Jordan: Thanks, appreciate it.
[11:08] Maya: Thanks everyone.
[11:10] Alex: Thanks — end.
